questions.prompt: A point \(x^\star\) is a global minimizer of \(f\) on a feasible set when
questions.explanation: Global means the comparison runs over the whole feasible set. The same comparison restricted to a ball is the local definition. The strict inequality for every other point, including infeasible ones, is stronger than the definition and uses the wrong set. A zero gradient is a calculus test for an interior candidate. It is not the definition of a minimizer, and it is not required at a boundary minimizer.
questions.figure_alt: A curve of one variable, drawn on labeled axes.
options: \(f(x^\star) \le f(x)\) for every feasible \(x\)
\(f(x^\star) \le f(x)\) for every feasible \(x\) in some ball around \(x^\star\)
\(f(x^\star) < f(x)\) for every \(x\) different from \(x^\star\), feasible or not
the gradient of \(f\) at \(x^\star\) is zero

questions.prompt: Let \(f(t) = (t - 2)^2 + 3\) on the whole real line. What is the global minimum value?
questions.explanation: The square is nonnegative and equals zero at \(t = 2\), so the smallest value is 3, attained at that single point. The minimizer is strict. Reporting 2 gives the minimizer, not the value. Reporting 0 gives the square at the minimizer and drops the added 3. Reporting 7 is \(f(0)\), which is larger.
questions.figure_alt: A curve of one variable, drawn on labeled axes.

questions.prompt: The minimizer \(t = 2\) of \(f(t) = (t - 2)^2 + 3\) is strict because
questions.explanation: Strict means no other feasible point ties the value. Here \(f(t) - 3 = (t - 2)^2 > 0\) for every \(t \ne 2\). A tie at a second point would make the minimizer non-strict. Openness of the domain is not the reason, and this function is never negative.
questions.figure_alt: A curve of one variable, drawn on labeled axes.
options: the domain is an open interval
every other real number has a strictly larger value
the value 3 is attained at two different points
the function is negative somewhere

questions.prompt: Let \(f(t) = (t^2 - 1)^2\) on the real line. Which statements hold?
questions.explanation:
The function is a square, so it is nonnegative, and it equals zero at \(t = \pm 1\). Those two points are global minimizers, and each is strict inside a small enough neighborhood that excludes the other.
• At \(t = 0\) the value is 1, and nearby points toward \(\pm 1\) have smaller values, so \(t = 0\) is not a local minimizer.
• At \(t = 2\) the value is 9. A small step \(h\) to the left gives \(f(2 - h) = (3 - 4h + h^2)^2\), and for every \(0 < h < 4\) that square is strictly less than 9. Every ball around \(t = 2\) contains such a step, so \(t = 2\) is not a local minimizer. The smaller value at the distant point \(t = 1\) is a global comparison and is not the reason.
questions.figure_alt: A curve of one variable, drawn on labeled axes.
options: \(t = 1\) is a local minimizer.
\(t = -1\) is a local minimizer.
\(t = 0\) is a local minimizer.
\(t = 2\) is a local minimizer.
Both \(t = 1\) and \(t = -1\) are global minimizers.

questions.prompt: Put these steps in the order used to certify a strict global minimizer.
questions.explanation: An infeasible point is not a minimizer, so feasibility comes first. The value at the candidate is the number every other point must beat. The comparison has to cover the whole feasible set, not a neighborhood, because the claim is global, and it has to be strict, because the claim is uniqueness. The argmin conclusion is the last sentence, after the comparison has been made. Checking a neighborhood only certifies a local minimizer.

questions.prompt: Let \(f(t) = e^{t} + 4\) on the whole real line. What is the infimum of \(f\)?
questions.explanation: The exponential is positive and gets arbitrarily close to 0, so \(f\) gets arbitrarily close to 4 and never reaches it or goes below it. The infimum is 4, and it is not a minimum: no minimizer exists. Reporting 5 uses \(f(0) = 1 + 4\). Reporting 1 uses the exponential at 0 and drops the shift.
questions.figure_alt: A curve of one variable, drawn on labeled axes.

questions.prompt: A note claims that \(f(t) = e^{t}\) attains a minimum on the real line. Exactly one step is false.
questions.explanation: The exponential is continuous and positive. A continuous function that hits its infimum does have a minimizer. The false step confuses an infimum with a value: getting arbitrarily close to 0 does not mean some input produces 0. The infimum is 0 and the range is the positive reals, so the minimum is not attained.
questions.figure_alt: A curve of one variable, drawn on labeled axes.
steps: The values get arbitrarily close to 0, so 0 is a value of the function.
A continuous function that attains a value equal to its infimum has a minimizer.
reasons: Getting arbitrarily close to 0 is not the same as equaling 0.
Hitting the infimum does not produce a minimizer.

questions.prompt: A non-strict global minimizer is a feasible point where the objective equals the optimal value and
questions.explanation: Non-strict means the inequality \(f(x^\star) \le f(x)\) holds for every feasible \(x\), and equality holds at some other feasible point. Each of those points is still a global minimizer, and each is a local minimizer. A positive gradient is a different test and is not part of the definition. A one-point feasible set cannot show a tie.

questions.prompt: The global minimizer of \((x - a)^2 + (y - b)^2\) is the point \((a, b)\). Write the squared Euclidean norm of that minimizer as an expression in a and b.
questions.explanation:
The two squares are nonnegative and vanish together only at \((a, b)\), so that point is the unique global minimizer and the minimum value is 0. Its squared distance to the origin is \(a^2 + b^2\).
• \(a + b\) adds the coordinates instead of squaring them.
• \((a + b)^2\) expands to \(a^2 + 2ab + b^2\), which is the square of the sum.
• \(a^2 - b^2\) subtracts the second square.

questions.prompt: A continuous function on a nonempty compact feasible set
questions.explanation: On a nonempty compact set in real space, a continuous function attains its infimum. That attained value is a global minimum, and every point where it is attained is a global minimizer, hence also a local one. The function is bounded on a compact set, so it cannot run off to \(-\infty\). Non-attainment needs a set that fails to be compact, or a function that fails to be continuous.

questions.prompt: Let \(f(t) = t^3 - 3t\) on the real line. The point \(t = 1\) is a local minimizer. What is \(f(1)\)?
questions.explanation: Substituting gives \(1 - 3 = -2\). The derivative \(3t^2 - 3\) vanishes at \(t = \pm 1\), and the second derivative \(6t\) is positive at \(t = 1\), so the point is a strict local minimizer. It is not global: \(f(t)\) goes to \(-\infty\) as \(t\) goes to \(-\infty\). Reporting 2 gives \(f(-1)\), the local maximum value. Reporting 1 gives the location, not the value. Reporting \(-3\) drops the cubic term.
questions.figure_alt: A curve of one variable, drawn on labeled axes.

questions.prompt: The argmin set of a function
questions.explanation: Any number of feasible points may share the optimal value, and then every one of them is a global minimizer. A finite infimum need not be attained, so the set can also be empty, and when it is nonempty it need not be a singleton. Stationary points include local maxima and saddles, which are not minimizers. Continuity does not by itself empty the argmin set.
